quote: Wie viel Scheiben {+mit Radius 1+} in ein Quadrat? (Asymptotisch [?] genau)
english: How many discs of radius 1 fit into a square? (asymptotically exact)
topic: The page completes an induction step (from n to n-1) in the proof of the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality, sketches a circuit for switching a current on and off independently from two or more places, and poses sphere-packing and circle-packing questions together with a related polygon minimization problem.

triage.modern_statement: Let N(s) be the largest number of non-overlapping closed discs of radius 1 that fit inside a square of side s. This is the same as the largest number of points with all mutual distances at least 2 that fit in a square of side s−2. The question asks for N(s) exactly, or at least its exact asymptotic behaviour as s→∞. The main term is N(s) ~ (π/√12)·s²/π = s²/(2√3), set by the density of the hexagonal packing. The finer question is the boundary correction, the term of order s, and the exact values for finite s.
triage.answered_by: The leading asymptotics follow from the theorem that the hexagonal packing is the densest circle packing in the plane. Axel Thue published a proof (dated 1890/1892, followed by a second one), which is generally considered incomplete. László Fejes Tóth gave the first rigorous proof in 1940. Boundary-corrected upper bounds for packings in bounded domains were later given by H. Groemer, among others. Exact optimal packings of n equal circles in a square have been proven only for small n, up to about 30, using computer-aided proofs (Nurmela–Östergård, Markót–Csendes and others). Larger n is still being studied numerically. I found no source linking Hilbert's note to his published problem lists. Packing questions do appear in his 18th problem, but that problem concerns space-filling and dense packing in general, not this finite-square question.

evidence.claim: Thue proved that the hexagonal lattice is the densest of all circle packings, but his original proof is generally believed to be incomplete.
L. Fejes Tóth gave the first rigorous proof of the optimality of the hexagonal packing in 1940.
The first rigorous proof of the optimal density among all packings, not just lattice packings, is attributed to László Fejes Tóth.

The problem is equivalent to finding the largest distance d such that n points can be placed in the square with all mutual distances at least d. All optimal packings of up to 20 circles had been determined exactly, and packings up to 50 were studied (Nurmela & Östergård, 1997).
Proven optimal packings of circles in a square are known up to n = 30. Survey by Szabó, Markót, Csendes et al.
Density upper bounds for packing equal circles in a square of side 1+d, citing Groemer's bound.
Circle packing in a square is a standard packing problem (the dual form: the smallest square containing n unit circles), and the problem is still being studied.
Recent work continues on dense packings of congruent circles in squares and other domains.

triage.why: Hilbert's note is the classical problem of packing equal circles in a square. The 'asymptotically exact' part is settled to first order: N(s) ~ s²/(2√3), which follows from Thue's theorem as rigorously proved by Fejes Tóth in 1940. Exact answers are proven only for small numbers of discs, and the precise lower-order and boundary behaviour is not fully determined. It remains an active area of computational and discrete geometry. Two limits on what I could check: my search budget ran out, so I could not confirm the exact form or citation of boundary-term results such as Groemer's (1960) or Oler's (1961) inequality. I also found no source connecting this note to Hilbert's published problems. Confidence is medium because the reading of the handwriting is marked uncertain ('[?]'), and the exact modern status of the boundary term is not fully confirmed by the sources I retrieved.
